name: dashu (dashu-int)
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add, sub, mul, div, gcd, hex conversion and small-value workloads, for operand sizes 10 to 10^4 bits, dashu-int versus ibig, num-bigint, malachite-nz and rug (GMP).
claimed_speedup: Small operands: ubig_add at 100 bits dashu 3.7 ns vs rug 21.9 ns; ubig_div at 100 bits 5.7 ns vs 32.4 ns; ubig_mul at 100 bits 22.6 ns vs 25.1 ns; ubig_gcd at 1000 bits 2.87 us vs 3.05 us. Report summary: dashu faster than rug in 98 of 153 small-value cases (one/two-word integers, 2-6x lower per-value overhead than GMP). rug/GMP is faster from about 1000 bits (ubig_mul at 10^4 bits: rug 4.52 us vs dashu 12.76 us).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp; criterion 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; optimisation profile not stated (cargo bench default assumed); dashu-int 0.4.2, rug 1.30.0 (GMP 6.x)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std, no C API (a Python binding exists), so use from C++ needs FFI work. Inline small-integer representation avoids GMP's per-value heap allocation, which is where it wins; large operands use slower algorithms than GMP.
caveats: The report calls itself 'quick, machine-specific local numbers, not authoritative' (one laptop, short measurement time). Bit-width sweep stops at 10^4 bits, so no large-operand comparison. The benchmark repo has 3 commits and 2 stars. A second independent suite (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, rug 1.24.1) shows GMP-backed rug far ahead of dashu on large workloads: digits of e at 10M digits rug 2.788 s vs dashu 19.943 s; Fibonacci at 100M rug 2.937 s vs dashu 26.224 s. Dashu descends from ibig; GitHub fork status not confirmed. Win is limited to small operands and gcd; optimisation profile unstated, so tier B not A.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): web search 'bigint benchmark Rust crates malachite rug GMP num-bigint ibig comparison results' -> DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks benchmark-report.md

name: Malachite
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add, sub, mul, div, gcd, extended gcd and conversions for 10 to 10^4 bits, malachite-nz 0.9.1 versus dashu, ibig, num-bigint and rug (GMP).
claimed_speedup: Tiny operands only: at 10 bits ubig_add malachite 2.1 ns vs rug 17.7 ns, ubig_mul 3.0 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_gcd 8.5 ns vs 20.9 ns, ubig_gcd_ext 25.8 ns vs 53.7 ns. At large sizes rug wins: ubig_mul at 10^4 bits malachite 8.28 us vs rug 4.52 us; ubig_gcd_ext at 1000 bits malachite 3.40 us vs rug 3.18 us.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp; criterion 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; optimisation profile not stated; malachite-nz 0.9.1, rug 1.30.0 (GMP 6.x)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std; LGPL-3.0 (GitHub page lists LGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0; -only/-or-later variant not confirmed). Parts derived from GMP, FLINT and MPFR. No C API, so C++ use needs FFI.
caveats: Malachite beats GMP only on one-to-two-word integers, where GMP's per-value allocation dominates. The same report tallies malachite as fastest in 27 of 205 cases versus rug 52, with rug ahead from about 1000 bits. The second suite (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, malachite 0.4.14 vs rug 1.24.1) has rug faster everywhere: digits of e at 10M digits rug 2.788 s vs malachite 3.689 s, Fibonacci at 100M rug 2.937 s vs malachite 5.192 s. Malachite's own site (malachite.rs) could not be opened, so no first-party claim recorded. Report is self-described as non-authoritative.

name: LibBF (Fabrice Bellard)
baseline: GNU MPFR (mpfr_mul, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate: GMP 6.3 / MPFR 4.2)
workload: Correctly rounded floating-point multiplication, addition, division and square root at 53 to 300,000 bits of precision, reported as ns per 64-bit limb.
claimed_speedup: Multiplication at 300,000-bit precision: libbf 51.2 ns/limb vs MPFR (rug) 78.9 ns/limb (about 1.5x faster, derived from page data). Not faster at 53-256 bits (43.4 vs 15.6 at 53 bits), at 3,000 bits (13.0 vs 9.4) or at 30,000 bits (43.0 vs 35.3); add, div and sqrt are slower than MPFR at every size listed.
compiler_and_flags: libbf version 2025-06-03 prebuilt bftest, clang -O2; rug 1.30.0 (gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1, GMP 6.3, MPFR 4.2) under rustc 1.96.1 --release
stars_or_usage: 19 stars (mirror); embedded in QuickJS for BigInt/BigFloat
tradeoffs: Small (about 90 KB compiled), no dependencies, SIMD-optimised NTT multiplication with near-linear running time, also decimal floats and IEEE semantics. Transcendental functions are much slower than MPFR (exp at 53 bits 2985 vs 518 ns/limb).
caveats: Win is limited to multiplication at very high precision on one Apple M4; MPFR is faster at every other operation and size in the same report. Measured by the author of libbeef, a competing Rust port, using libbf's own bftest harness; libbf operands come from a run-length random generator with sizes uniform in [1, 2*prec] bits while rug used full-width operands, so the comparison is not perfectly like-for-like. libbf's own README calls it 'not the fastest library' and says about 4x slower than TachusPI on pi. The upstream site bellard.org/libbf was blocked, so the GitHub mirror (rurban/libbf, tarball releases with CI fixes) is cited; its last commit is 2025-08-19.

name: CGBN (Cooperative Groups Big Numbers, XMP 2.0)
baseline: GNU GMP 6.1.2 with OpenMP on a 20-core Xeon
workload: Batched fixed-size unsigned multiple-precision operations (add, sub, mul low, Montgomery reduce, modular exponentiation with odd modulus, div_qr, sqrt, gcd, modular inverse) at 128 to 8192 bits, one V100 GPU versus 20 Xeon cores.
claimed_speedup: add 28.6x-174.3x (average 77.4x); mul (low) 14.6x-172.9x (average 43.5x); mont_reduce average 29.3x; powm_odd 16.8x-24.6x (average 21.4x); div_qr 7.8x-30.0x (average 14.4x); sqrt average 11.3x; gcd 3.1x-8.4x (average 6.9x); mod inv 2.5x-5.6x (average 4.1x).
compiler_and_flags: not stated (README says results come from the perf_tests tools in the repo; GMP 6.1.2 with OpenMP)
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 (Volta) GPU versus Intel Xeon E5-2698v4 20-core at 2.2 GHz
tradeoffs: GPU-only (CUDA), fixed-size unsigned integers decided at compile time (32 to 32K bits in 32-bit steps, 4/8/16/32 threads per number), useful only for large batches of independent operations; GMP and Google Test are needed for the tests. NVIDIA fork steleman/nvidia-cgbn adds signed integers, Ada/Blackwell support and sizes up to 256K bits.
caveats: First-party README table, GPU versus CPU, so it measures a different class of hardware rather than a better algorithm on equal hardware. Compiler and flags not stated; GMP 6.1.2 is old. Labelled 'XMP 2.0 Beta Release (Oct 2018)'. License inferred from the MIT-style text in the LICENSE file (GitHub page did not display an SPDX id).

name: gnu-mpfr-cgbn (MPFR with CUDA/CGBN acceleration)
baseline: GNU MPFR 4.2.1 (scalar, one core) with GMP 6.3.0
workload: Batched correctly rounded mpfr_mul, fma, div, sqrt, add at 128 to 65536 bits, comparing scalar CPU MPFR with batch (PCIe transfers included) and device-resident GPU execution.
claimed_speedup: mpfr_mul at 8192 bits, 16384 operations: CPU 4.757 us/op, batch 0.728 us/op (6.5x), device-resident 0.0167 us/op (284.1x). Peak batch figures at 1024 operations: div 30.4x and sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits, mul 21.2x at 49152 bits, fma 18.3x at 40960 bits. A single operation always loses (n=1 rows 0.0x-0.4x).
compiler_and_flags: NVCC -O3 -arch=sm_120 -Xcompiler -fPIC; CUDA 13.2, driver 595.71.05; MPFR 4.2.1, GMP 6.3.0; host compiler flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120, 82 SMs, 2.41 GHz, 31.4 GiB); CPU baseline 'one core, the same machine' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Results identical to stock MPFR (same rounded value, ternary value and exception flags in all five rounding modes). Needs a CUDA GPU and large batches; precision above 65536 bits runs on the CPU; division and sqrt above 32768 bits are slower than the CPU. Sweet spot 4096-16384 bits with batches of a few thousand.
caveats: First-party benchmark on one GPU, GPU versus one CPU core (CPU model unstated), so not an equal-hardware comparison. The 284x figure is for device-resident data with no transfer; with transfers the best is about 6.5x for that case. Addition never wins in batch mode (at most 0.7x). Repository has a single commit (2026-09-12), so it is new and unproven. Built on GNU MPFR 4.2.1 sources; GitHub page lists LGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0.

name: blip_mp
workload: Arbitrary-precision integer add, sub, mul, divMod, powm at i64-range values and 128 to 32768-bit operands, including RSA-size multiplication, division and modular exponentiation, versus GMP with and without assembly.
claimed_speedup: All i64-fitting values 1.95-2.66x faster than GMP; mul at 1024/2048/3072 bits 1.19-1.45x faster; RSA-2048 trifecta mul 1.16x, divMod 1.31x, powm 1.11x (elsewhere the README says RSA-2048 powm 13% faster and 2048/1024-bit division 24% faster); add at 768 bits and above 1.04-1.28x faster; sub at 256 bits and above 1.03-2.11x faster.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast, libc malloc, GMP built via Nix (also a --disable-assembly GMP variant); benchmark run by nix build .#bench / blip_mp_bench
hardware: Apple Silicon M-series (exact chip not stated), aarch64-darwin; cross-check on AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS (Zen 4) laptop under NixOS
tradeoffs: Pure Zig with a C FFI, variable-length self-describing 'BLIP' byte encoding with small-buffer optimisation, no inline assembly. Integers only (no mpf, mpq or MPFR-class floats); FFT multiplication exists but is gated off.
caveats: First-party, 3-run hand medians, M-series chip not named, so tier C. README license line reads 'MIT or Apache-2.0 (TBD before tagging a release)' and no LICENSE file was found, so license recorded as null and usability as reference. Loses to GMP at 128-bit add/sub (0.56-0.65x), 16384+ bit multiplication (0.55-0.87x) and modular inverse (2.5-4x slower). On x86-64 Zen 4 GMP's assembly is 1.65-3.88x faster than GMP without assembly and blip_mp loses the large sizes to it by 1.5-4x; the headline wins are Apple Silicon only. README figures are not fully consistent (powm 1.11x vs 13%; 13029 vs 8240 cross-checks). Project started 2026-05-16.

name: MultiFloats.jl
workload: Extended-precision (128-256 bit, 30-60 digit) floating-point +, -, *, /, sqrt using unevaluated sums of Float64 values, compared with Julia BigFloat (MPFR), Quadmath.jl and DoubleFloats.jl.
claimed_speedup: At 30-digit precision, 30x faster than BigFloat, 6x faster than Quadmath.jl and 2x faster than DoubleFloats.jl.
tradeoffs: Fixed 128-256 bits only (Float64x2-x4, Float32x2-x4), not arbitrary precision. Not correctly rounded; treats +-Inf inputs as NaN; transcendental functions call MPFR. Julia only.
caveats: README gives ratios without hardware, Julia version or table; the benchmark gist (gist.github.com/dzhang314/3e10463843f4ab5f5a4a2206c877771b, QR of 400x400 and pseudoinverse of 250x400 at 106 bits) has code but no recorded output on the page. README cites peer-reviewed papers (SC25, CAV25) that were not opened. Compared against MPFR only indirectly through Julia's BigFloat, which allocates on every operation; a C++ double-double library would be the like-for-like rival.

name: TzdLanguage NTT BigInt multiplier
workload: Multiplication of two 4,741,006-digit integers using a 3-prime NTT with Garner CRT on CPU (AVX2) and GPU (CUDA).
claimed_speedup: Pure multiply: CPU AVX2 NTT 54.02 ms vs single-core GMP 111.78 ms (2.07x); GPU NTT 29.20 ms (3.83x); 8-thread GMP 84.58 ms. End-to-end including decimal conversion 175.41 ms CPU and 56.52 ms GPU vs GMP 2,549.30 ms (14.5x and 45.1x).
hardware: Intel Core i7-4790 (4C/8T, 3.60 GHz); NVIDIA P106-090 GPU (Pascal, 192 GB/s)
tradeoffs: The NTT multiplier lives inside a programming-language interpreter (src files TzdExperimentalCompute.cpp for the CPU engine, TzdPyTorch.cpp for the GPU engine) and surfaces through language-level operations, not as a standalone library; extracting it takes work. Single operand size tested.
caveats: First-party README with a single data point, compiler and flags not stated. The end-to-end speedups mostly reflect GMP's decimal string conversion (GMP end-to-end 2,549 ms vs 111.78 ms pure multiply). The repository's commit history spans only about 17 days (2026-09-13 to 2026-09-30). The 'multi-threaded GMP' row is not a standard GMP feature and its method is not described. The relevant wiki pages (wiki/CPU-NTT-BigInt.md, GPU-NTT-BigInt.md) were not opened.

name: DoubleFloats.jl
workload: Vector (1000 values) and 50x50 matrix operations in 85+ bit double-double arithmetic (Double64) versus Float128 (libquadmath) and BigFloat set to 128 bits of precision.
claimed_speedup: Relative time, smaller is faster, Double64 = 1 versus Big128 (BigFloat/MPFR): dot(v,v) 7, v .+ v 16, v .* v 25, exp.(m) 6, m * m 9, det(m) 11.
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkTools; Julia version and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Fixed ~106-bit (85+ accurate bits) double-double, exponent range of Float64, not arbitrary precision and not correctly rounded; transcendental functions accurate to about 1e-31. Julia only.
caveats: Table in the README has no hardware, Julia version or absolute times, only relative ratios. Compares against MPFR only through Julia's allocating BigFloat. The same-class C++ library is QD (double-double/quad-double), which would be the like-for-like comparison. MultiFloats.jl (separate entry) claims to be 2x faster than DoubleFloats.jl.

name: ibig
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add, sub, mul, div at 10 to 10^4 bits, ibig 0.3.6 versus dashu, num-bigint, malachite-nz and rug (GMP).
claimed_speedup: At 10 bits: ubig_add ibig 1.8 ns vs rug 17.7 ns, ubig_sub 1.5 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_mul 2.1 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_div 1.5 ns vs 28.3 ns. At 10^4 bits GMP wins: ubig_mul rug 4.52 us vs ibig 12.69 us.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp; criterion 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; optimisation profile not stated
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std, inline small-integer representation; no subquadratic gcd (10-13x slower than dashu/malachite/rug at 10^4 bits), no C API.
caveats: Win over GMP is confined to one-word integers (about 10 bits in the sweep); from about 1000 bits rug is ahead. The benchmarked version is ibig 0.3.6 while the repository now requires rustc 1.95 and carries an ibig-old directory, so the current code may differ. In the second suite (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, rug 1.24.1) ibig is far behind rug on large workloads (digits of e at 10M: rug 2.788 s vs ibig 20.673 s). Dashu, a fork of ibig, is reported as its own entry. Report self-described as non-authoritative.
